title: BTS Chooses Not to Submit to the Grammys After New Asian Pop Category Announced
summary: Why K-pop group BTS will not be submitting their music to next year’s Grammy Awards, the members announced July 28.
story: K-pop group BTS will not be submitting their music to next year’s Grammy Awards, the members announced July 28.
The group — made up of members RM, Jimin, V, Suga, Jungkook, Jin and J-Hope — shared the same statement on their individual Instagram stories.

The announcement comes just over a month after the Recording Academy — the body of musicians, producers, engineers and more that vote on the awards, announced five new categories — including a “Best Asian Pop Music Performance,” which would include K-pop among other genres.

“We have decided not to enter the Grammys this year,” reads a translation of the message, which was written in Korean. “I hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language.”

In a statement shared with TODAY.com, Grammys CEO Harvey Mason Jr. said that he was “saddened” to hear BTS’ decision, but understood and respected the choice. Mason also said that artists who submit to a genre category — such as Asian pop, jazz or country — are not excluded from also submitting to, and being considered in, the general field categories. These categories include record of the year, album of the year and song of the year.

“Those categories remain open to any eligible recording, regardless of genre,” Mason said in the statement. “Recognition in a genre category and recognition in the General Field are not mutually exclusive. An artist can absolutely pursue both.”
Mason also said that the Asian pop category was “created to celebrate the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth” of pop music out of Asia.
“More categories mean more artists’ work is recognized,” Mason said in the statement.

According to the Academy’s description of the new categories, which was announced on June 16, the best Asian pop music performance would recognize performances “originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets.” This would include K-pop, J-pop, C-pop and more, and involve the “meaningful use of one or more Asian languages.”

BTS, which stands for Bangtan Sonyeondan, or Bulletproof Boy Scouts, would have been able to submit work off of their newest album “Arirang,” which came out in March. The album marks the group’s first album together after each of the members completed their mandatory military service in Korea.

The group has a special spot in Grammys history. In 2019, they became the first K-pop act to present at the prestigious awards show. The group, which presented the best R&B album, had the honor of handing the award to winner H.E.R. for her self-titled album.
“Growing up in South Korea, we always dreamed of being on the Grammys stage,” said bandmember RM, according to Variety. “Thank you to all our fans for making this dream come true and we’ll be back.”

A year later, they became the first K-pop act to perform at the awards show, putting on a stunning performance alongside rapper Lil Nas X for the hit “Old Town Road.” And in 2022, they performed the hit single “Butter,” which has racked up more than 115 million views on YouTube alone.

They’ve also earned five Grammy award nominations, including three for best pop duo/group performance and one best music video nod for 2013’s “Yet to Come (The Most Beautiful Moment).” While they were the first K-pop group to receive any Grammy nods, they have yet to win an award.

Most recently, the group made headlines for their performance at the World Cup Finals halftime show on July 19. Dressed in black, white and red coordinating ensembles, BTS took over the pitch with an electrifying performance of their song “Dynamite.”

title: ‘Tony’ Reviews: Here’s What Critics Are Saying About the Anthony Bourdain Biopic
summary: Here’s what critics are saying about the Anthony Bourdain biopic, “Tony.”
story: Anthony Bourdain takes center stage in “Tony,” a biopic of the late chef and author.

In the film, Dominic Sessa, known for his work in the Academy Award-winning 2023 comedy-drama “The Holdovers,” as well as 2025’s “Now You See Me: Now You Don’t,” fills the role of a young, blunt Bourdain. The film, directed by Matt Johnson, also stars Antonio Banderas, Emilia Jones and Leo Woodall.
Bourdain died by suicide in 2018, yet the author — who wrote bestselling 2000 book “Kitchen Confidential,” which rocketed him to stardom — continues to inspire fans to this day.
“Tony” takes moviegoers back to a 19-year-old Bourdain in the summer of 1975, when he worked at a seafood restaurant in Cape Cod, Massachusetts.
The film, which has a 100% score on Rotten Tomatoes as of July 29, opens Aug. 7 and is poised to take a bite out of the box office.
Thinking of checking it out? Here’s what the critics are saying.
The Hollywood Reporter
“A slender slice of a famous life, the movie feels a little wispy in its mix of scrappy and sweet, rough-edged and yet bathed in the balming glow of nostalgia,” David Rooney writes.
“But it has an idiosyncratic charm that fits the title character, without ever sanding down the abrasive side of a chronic liar or masking his insecurities.”
Rooney also praised Sessa’s performance.

“Making good on his promise in ‘The Holdovers,’ Dominic Sessa is excellent in the role, nailing the contradictory aspects of a slippery character while mapping his coming-of-age arc with empathy and honesty,” he writes.
“There’s no dark foreshadowing of the tragedy we know will come 43 years later — only chutzpah, raw potential and intermittent flickers of vulnerability.”
The Daily Beast

Nick Schager’s review echoed the sentiment that Sessa holds his own in the film, noting it “becomes more convincing and authentic with each passing scene, it has a rough-around-the-edges charm that’s in keeping with its go-for-broke protagonist.”
Schager also cites the film’s “spontaneity and genuineness” and lauds Banderas’ work.

“‘Tony’ swings and sways like a lobster boat in choppy waters off the New England coast, and though that setting would seem to be an unlikely place to find Antonio Banderas, the star makes for a delightful boss and, eventually, mentor,” he writes.

Schager says “Tony” serves as a “prologue” for the success Bourdain would later find, calling it a “tad slight” when considering the rich life Bourdain eventually led. However, the film is successful when assessed in its own “limited terms.”
“It may be little more than a tease that leads viewers to Bourdain’s copious written and screen works, but as far as amuse-bouches go, ‘Tony’ is a memorably tasty one,” he writes.
Variety
Owen Gleiberman opens his review, pondering “what Bourdain himself would have made of the movie.”
“To me, if an Anthony Bourdain biopic can’t clear the bar called ‘Bourdain would have liked it,’ it’s probably not a good movie,” he continues. “‘Tony’ clears that bar.”
He also applauds Johnson’s directorial effort.

“‘Tony’ has been framed as the origin story of how Anthony Bourdain became Anthony Bourdain,” he writes. “But one of the many things that Matt Johnson ... understands is that Anthony — or, as he called himself then, Tony — already was Anthony Bourdain.”
Gleiberman said the film marks a watershed moment for Sessa.

“To me, one of the most pleasurable things in movies is that moment when you see an actor become a movie star,” he writes “That’s what happens to Dominic Sessa in ‘Tony.’ I don’t care if the film is a summer indie smash or not (though it deserves to be) — it shows you that Sessa has the goods.”
The Wrap
William Bibbiani’s review begins by comparing “Tony” to “The Social Network,” explaining how the biopic understands “how to really make us care about” a person who is not necessarily appealing.
“‘Tony’ never makes young Bourdain entirely likable,” he writes later.

“This isn’t a superhero origin story where he changes and becomes a do-gooder at the end,” he continues. “This is an origin story about Bourdain’s inciting incident, the exact moment in his life where he realized he needed to change. In Matt Johnson’s hands, that’s epic enough for a whole film.”
Still, the movie left him feeling somewhat hollow.

“By the time the credits roll, ‘Tony’ has long since receded in a formula,” he writes. “The big finale feels contrived and a little unconvincing. I guess the filmmakers thought subverting the tone of a biopic was enough, so Johnson throws Bourdain’s fan base a bone. It just doesn’t have any meat on it.”
The film, Bibbiani goes on to write, does however earn the viewer’s affection — “mostly because it never pretends Bourdain has.”

“We are invited to view the genius as a work in progress. Bourdain’s rough draft stinks; the film about this rough draft is polished and interesting, but another round of notes wouldn’t have killed it,” he writes. “We’re watching a guy who will one day reach his full potential, in a movie that doesn’t entirely reach its own.”
Associated Press
Mark Kennedy’s opening paragraph takes a big swing at a missed opportunity.
“Like all first courses, it leaves you with a nice first taste — but still hungry,” he writes.
Kennedy writes that the film’s director and co-writer Matt Johnson took “liberties with a formative period in Bourdain’s life.”
However, he “still only manages to tell the story of how a callow lad became somewhat of a less callow lad after toiling in a restaurant kitchen on Cape Cod in 1975,” Kennedy writes.
Kennedy laments how this picture could’ve been even better.
“In ‘Tony,’ the world-weary, forever romantic, noodle-slurping Bourdain that we would fall in love with decades later via travel shows like “Parts Unknown” stays firmly out of grasp,” he writes.
Kennedy also asks whether it was necessary to place Bourdain at the center of this film.
“Who doesn’t like a good coming of age?” Kennedy writes. “Why did it have to be Bourdain if Bourdain never gets to be Bourdain?”
ScreenRant
Matt Harrison credits the film, which he calls “laugh-out-loud funny” for making an entertaining flick with Bourdain as the central character.
“It works on its own terms, with or without the halo of its subject’s career. It’s actually about something. And it’s a delight to watch,” he writes.
“It’s sincerely interested in who this lost 19-year-old thinks he is, who he actually is, and who he’s going to choose to become,” he adds.

Harrison, who calls the film “thoroughly enjoyable,” also singled out how the scenes in the kitchen feel “truly alive.” And Sessa “can embody all the epigraph’s unlikable traits and remain remarkably easy to root for.”
IndieWire
“‘Tony’ retains the sincere flavor of street meat despite being factory-processed within an inch of its life,” David Ehrlich writes.
He also salutes Sessa’s “wholly self-possessed lead performance” and how Johnson framed one of the early and key parts of Bourdain’s journey.

“Johnson recognizes how this, at heart, is a coming-of-age story about a rising star who’s learning to be unburdened by a future that’s better than he could ever imagine — a kid who’s learning that no one can become the person they pretend to be without being the person they actually are along the way,” he writes.
“‘Tony’ struggles for an ending, but it doesn’t really need one; the real fun here lies in paving the way to parts unknown.”

title: The Nickname Robert Pattinson’s Daughter Has For ‘The Batman’ Star Is Too Cute
summary: Musician Suki Waterhouse said that her 2-year-old daughter, whom she shares with fiancé Robert Pattinson, isn’t really bothered by Pattinson’s slightly scary costume and makeup that he wears while playing Batman.
story: Musician Suki Waterhouse said that her 2-year-old daughter, whom she shares with fiancé Robert Pattinson, isn’t really bothered by Pattinson’s slightly scary costume and makeup that he wears while playing Batman.
In fact, it seems the toddler is embracing her dad’s alter-ego.
During an appearance on a recent episode of the “And The Writer Is” podcast, Waterhouse, 34, revealed the sweet nickname the toddler uses when she sees Pattinson, 40, as the vigilante.
“She calls him, like, ‘Daddy Batman’ now because he’s always dressed up like that for the next seven months whenever he’s on FaceTime,” said the singer, who gave birth to the baby girl in 2024.
During the podcast episode, Waterhouse opened up about being a mom, revealing how her daughter processes her parents’ unique jobs.
The couple have not publicly revealed their daughter’s name.

The songwriter told host fellow musician Ross Golan that her daughter understands that Waterhouse is a musician and that her dad dons a cape and mask to portray Batman. She shared the funny moment that she and her daughter had on FaceTime with Pattinson, who called them from the set of the long-anticipated “The Batman” sequel, “The Batman Part II,” which is currently in production.
“She’s on FaceTime to her dad who today is covered in blood with huge black circles around his eyes and I’m like, ‘Hi, is it fine?’ And we’re just like, ‘It’s fine,’” she told Golan.

While Pattinson is away filming, Waterhouse has been enjoying some mother-daughter bonding time. She shared on the podcast that she and her daughter were flipping through a book the other day, when the toddler spotted a girl holding a guitar.
“She was like, ‘That’s your job,’” she recalled to Golan.
Waterhouse said her daughter had been watching her play guitar and practice her set as she prepared for her “Loveland Tour,” which kicked off on July 22 in Phoenix, Arizona.
“She’ll say, like, ‘mommy songs’ (and) I’ll show her my music videos and stuff and so it’s cool,” she continued.
Waterhouse added that her daughter enjoys sitting in on glam sessions with her hair and makeup team and looking at the different nail polish options.
Waterhouse and Pattinson, who were first spotted together in 2018, have both opened up about their family and the experience of raising a daughter.
When Waterhouse stopped by TODAY in December 2024, she gushed that she was “completely and utterly besotted” with her baby girl.
“I didn’t know that it would be this good,” she said.
After her appearance, she spoke with TODAY.com and talked about how excited she was to be taking her daughter on tour for the first time.
She explained, “There’s so many hours before you get on stage of walking around, being in a different city — doing that with her will be amazing.”
Waterhouse also shared that her favorite moment of the day was playing in the pool with her daughter and fiancé.

“We have, like, a routine of putting her in the swimming pool and jumping in and out of the pool,” she said. “That’s just always the most fun, like, end of the day, 5 p.m., we all get in the pool and be silly. It’s amazing.”
Pattinson has also talked about parenthood, discussing how he has grown since becoming a father in an interview with Icon Magazine published in October 2025.
The proud dad said, “I have so much more patience. It’s funny, it’s not even patience; I genuinely enjoy hanging out with babies. That surprised me.”

He playfully added, “It’s also funny how you start having real, normie conversations — about things like schools or daycares… it’s so strange. It’s like, there’s this gravitational pull…Like, I have to wear Patagonia puffer jackets and cargo shorts now. I just have to.”

title: What Happens to Drew Starkey’s Character Cary in ‘Lucky’?
summary: Does Cary die in Lucky? What happens to Cary in Lucky? Here’s a recap of Episode 4 of the Apple TV series “Lucky”.
story: Warning: Spoilers ahead for “Lucky.”

“You’re alive. Good for you,” are the first words Lucky utters to her husband Cary after finding him hiding out in a luxurious beachside home while she has been fighting to survive ever since he left.

“Lucky,” the Apple TV miniseries based on Marissa Stapley’s novel of the same name starring Anya Taylor-Joy as the titular character, opened with the protagonist being abandoned by her husband, played by Drew Starkey, after the two stole $10 million and planned to run off together.

In the first three episodes of the crime thriller, Lucky is on the run, dodging the FBI and her mother-in-law Priscilla, (Annette Bening) who happens to be a crime boss. The con artist is looking for answers, too, as she tries to track down her deceitful spouse and figure out why he betrayed her.

Her answers arrive in Episode 4, out July 29, when Lucky and Cary come face-to-face for the first time. During an intense and bloody confrontation, Cary reveals why he left his wife confused and alone, and what happened to the money. His revelation leads to a heartbreaking scene at the end of the episode that sets up Lucky’s journey for the rest of the season.
Read on to find out where Cary has been and what happens to his character below.
Why Did Cary Leave Lucky?

When Cary walks into his hideout and finds his scorned wife waiting for him, he admits he knew she would track him down. He attempts to explain his actions and make amends. But she isn’t interested at first, instead punching him in the face after he approaches her.

Lucky berates him for leaving her scared and vulnerable and accuses him of never loving her. He apologizes and assures her their relationship is real. He reveals that he left because his mom planned to kill Lucky.

We learn in a flashback scene that Cary previously visited his mom and she shared that she knew Lucky had stolen millions from her. Priscilla also learned that Lucky had turned her in to the FBI, sending her to prison for years. Cary calls Lucky out for keeping that secret from him throughout their marriage.

Despite feeling hurt, Cary still wanted to protect his wife. So, he drugged her after their night out in Las Vegas, took the money and left their hotel room in the wee hours of the morning. When he reached his mom, he changed his mind and decided to return to Lucky. But when he arrived at the hotel, he saw the building was surrounded by police and drove away.
Cary took the money and deposited most of it into a Bitcoin account, protected by a seed phrase. He used the rest of the money to purchase his secret spot in La Jolla, California.

When Lucky asks for the phrase and he refuses, she threatens to shoot him. Before she can pull the trigger, the FBI, led by Agent Billie Rand (Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor), bang on the door and demand Cary come outside.
Does Lucky Forgive Cary?
As the FBI enter, Lucky and Cary flee in their getaway car.

A high-speed hunt ensues through the streets of San Diego. Just when Cary and Lucky think they have evaded the authorities, they run into Priscilla, who also starts chasing them. Then, the police are on their trail again.
Possibly facing death, Lucky confesses to her husband that she still loves him. “I don’t regret us,” she tells him.
“Neither do I,” he replies.
Does Cary Die?
Unfortunately, yes.

Cary decides to slow down the police by leaning out the window and attempting to shoot the tires of the cop cars. He and the police exchange fire. When one of the tires on Cary and Lucky’s car is shot, the vehicle flips over multiple times.
Lucky awakes and sees that while Cary survived the crash, he was shot by one of the officers. She tries to stop the bleeding and keep him alive, but it doesn’t work.
“You were happy…” he tells her before his eyes close and he dies.
What Will Happen in Episode 5?
With no time to mourn the death of her husband, Lucky sneaks out of the vehicle and goes on the run once more.

With only three episodes remaining, including the finale out on Aug. 19, viewers will see if Lucky will manage to stay alive and how she will retrieve the money now that Cary died without sharing the seed phrase.
Plus, viewers will likely watch Lucky and Priscilla face off and see how she’ll get help from her dad John (Timothy Olyphant) despite him being in prison.
Episode 5, titled “Are We Bad People?” will be released on Aug. 5.

title: Fabien Frankel Talks Shocking ‘House of the Dragon’ Twist: ‘I Knew I Had it Coming’
summary: Fabien Frankel talks his character Criston Cole meeting his bloody demise in “The Butcher’s Ball” on TODAY.
story: Warning: This post contains spoilers for “House of the Dragon.”
Fabien Frankel’s Criston Cole fulfilled his wish of dying “the realm’s greatest warrior” when met his bloody demise in “House of the Dragon.”
Minutes into Season 3, Episode 6 of “House of the Dragon,” entitled “The Butcher’s Ball,” Ser Cole led his men onto a battlefield that he thought was filled with deceased soldiers.

But his enemies were simply tricking him and arose, launching a sudden attack. Although Cole begged for his life and tried to surrender, his pleas were ignored and he died after being hit by multiple arrows.

It was an honorable death for Cole, and one he didn’t fear. In the episode prior, he said in a monologue, “I have been a servant all my life, to Green or to Black. I have defined myself by oaths, through unyielding devotion. And the highborn have made much of me while it pleased them to do so. But I will not let them diminish me now. I will not return spurned, rejected. I am the realm’s greatest warrior. And I will die as such.”
During an appearance on TODAY July 29, Frankel opened up about his character’s death.

“I knew I had it coming. I’d done so much bad stuff. I knew at some point I’d get a call saying our time was up. I lived a life. I did a lot of episodes. It was a good, long journey,” Frankel said on TODAY.
Frankel said he would “do a bit” with his friends about coming back for the show’s next season, even though his character’s fate was clearly spelled out in the book that inspired the show.

“I kept doing a while bit where I’d say, ‘I gotta go back next year, do a whole new season of the show.’ My friends were like, ‘You’re really lying directly to my face,’” he said. “I feel that’s apt for Criston and apt for myself.”
Frankel also described the “outpouring” he’s witnessed since his character’s death.
“There’s more love for Criston now than I felt ... now that he’s not alive, people maybe feel a little bit worse about hating him so much,” he said with a smile.
Cole, a divisive character, had appeared on the fantasy series since it premiered in 2022.

A day after the death of his character aired, Frankel posted a tribute to Cole on Instagram. Beside a carousel of behind-the-scenes photos taken on the set of the HBO series, Frankel wrote in the caption, “3 seasons. 21 episodes. 5 and half years. A badly dealt with heartbreak.”
He added, “To all of you who tuned in every week, And to all those who have carried me along the way, I couldn’t have gotten through it without you. It’s been an honour. Criston Cole, over and out.”
Fans complimented Frankel’s performance on the show in the comments.
“Hated your character which means you are a spectacular actor sir,” one said.
Another agreed and wrote, “A sign of a great actor is that they can make you hate them on screen. You were up there with some of the most hated in the GoT universe and we love you for that!”
The official HBO account also left a message that read, “We thank you for your valiant service to the crown, Ser Fabien.”

title: U.S. agrees to pause attacks on Iran subject to ‘rapidly’ making deal, Trump says
summary: The U.S. has agreed to pause attacks on Iran, President Donald Trump said Saturday, amid what he said were the “perimeters of a deal” being agreed upon, which would include the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
story: The U.S. has agreed to pause attacks on Iran, President Donald Trump said Saturday, amid what he said were the “perimeters of a deal” being agreed upon, which would include the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

“We have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s  nuclear threat.”
The president said the U.S. was “locked and loaded and ready to go” against Iran but that he agreed to cancel attacks “subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL.”
He added that Israel, the U.S. partner in the war with Iran, “joins me in this commitment.”
“Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE,” Trump said of a possible new agreement.

The statement came after the State Department on Saturday urged Americans across the Middle East to consider leaving the region or be prepared to depart on short notice. It also warned of flight disruptions and security risks as the conflict with Iran appeared to be escalating.

Trump earlier threatened Iran with additional attacks, saying Friday that the U.S. will be “hitting them very hard,” while Iran has vowed to “punish” the U.S. and both nations traded what some U.S. officials described as “heavy” strikes.
Responding to Trump’s announcement, Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told “Meet the Press” Sunday that the president should not trust Iran’s word.
Asked why a fresh deal would be different when the Memorandum of Understanding signed in June failed, he told moderator Kristen Welker: “Well, it may not be.”
“We only have three choices: escalate, retreat and come home, or maintain the status quo. I would maintain the status quo as long as I could,” he said.
Iran’s acting minister of defense, Iran Majid Ibn al-Reza, meanwhile said that U.S. remarks should be viewed as “psychological and cognitive warfare.”
He said on X that the threat of further strikes would be taken “as the basis for increasing readiness, strengthening deterrence, and enhancing our own power.”

Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman, a key regional player, spoke with Trump by phone Saturday. According to the Saudi state news agency, he told him that dialogue was needed to de-escalate Middle East tensions, and expressed concerns over plans for new strikes against Iran.
The State Department issued fresh security guidance Saturday for Americans in the region.

“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions,” the State Department said. “Some airlines in the region have postponed resumption of earlier flight schedules; others have cancelled some routes. Americans in the region should consider departing, or be prepared to depart should there be escalation.”
The State Department also urged Americans to reconsider travel bans to or through the region.
The warning was distributed through U.S. embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar and Saudi Arabia.

The agency posted a nearly identical statement earlier this month, but that bulletin did not urge Americans to prepare to leave the Middle East or to reconsider upcoming trips, reflecting Washington’s growing concern that the conflict could widen.
On Saturday, the Kuwait Army said its air defense systems intercepted drone attacks from Iran.

“Kuwaiti air defenses are currently engaging hostile drone attacks following the Iranian aggression. The General Staff of the Army notes that any explosions heard are a result of air defense systems intercepting the hostile attacks,” the army said.

Two days ago, the U.S. military confirmed it had executed a “heavy wave of strikes” on Iran, hours after Fox News reported that the president in a phone call had vowed to “beat the f-----g s--- out of” the country.
Trump has grown increasingly exasperated with the state of the war, one Trump ally told NBC News.
“There was not a real strategy for how long or what they should do to get to the endpoint,” the ally said.
The conflict has now entered its sixth month, despite Trump’s repeated early predictions that the war would resolve itself “shortly.”
The protracted conflict has led to soaring oil prices globally and rising gas prices in the U.S.
There was a brief reprieve from fighting in June when the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding outlining the process for talks to end the war.
But in early July, Trump declared a ceasefire to be “over” and the countries resumed striking targets in the Middle East.

title: Hackers targeted municipal water systems in 7 states this week, FBI says
summary: Cyberattacks targeting municipal water systems have been reported in at least seven states this week, prompting the FBI and the Environmental Protection Agency to warn utilities nationwide that hackers are trying to disrupt critical water infrastructure.
story: Cyberattacks targeting municipal water systems have been reported in at least seven states this week, prompting the FBI and the Environmental Protection Agency to warn utilities nationwide that hackers are trying to disrupt critical water infrastructure.

In a public service announcement Thursday, the agencies said water and wastewater utilities have reported incidents to the FBI, with some malicious activity degrading water operations. The announcement does not name the states.

The warning comes after hackers targeted more than 30 municipal water facilities in Minnesota in an attack that had hallmarks of Iranian meddling, according to a law enforcement official. It is still under investigation.

A spokesperson for Minnesota’s information technology services agency said Thursday there was no indication the breaches contaminated any municipal water supplies. The federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said in a separate alert that some larger attacks on water infrastructure had “resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations,” though it did not say where.

Minnesota officials and the U.S. government have not publicly attributed the malicious activity in the state to a specific actor. Likewise, the FBI and the EPA did not identify a culprit behind the breaches in the other states.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters Friday at Camp David, blamed Minnesota’s leaders and Gov. Tim Walz, who was the Democratic vice presidential nominee in the 2024 election.

“I think I blame it on Minnesota because they’re grossly incompetent,” Trump said. “I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota. They like to say, ‘Oh, it’s Iran.’ Iran should be so lucky. Iran’s got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota.”

In response to a request for comment, Walz said in part: “Trump knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too. This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there’s no plan to win a war with Iran.”
The FBI and EPA advisory focused less on attribution than on the tactics used in the attacks.

The federal advisory said the malicious cyber actors, or MCAs, targeted specific brands of control systems used by municipal water utilities, though the FBI and the EPA urged operators of all systems to take precautions.

Earlier this week, the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources issued a bulletin to water contacts in the state, saying  intelligence officials believed that “systems within Wisconsin may be susceptible to connections from malicious cyber actors.”
“This leads us to believe that the cyber threat is ongoing in Wisconsin and requires immediate action to prevent potentially serious impacts to our systems,” the bulletin said.

A Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources spokesperson emphasized that intelligence officials in the state “had not yet confirmed that systems in Wisconsin have had connections but are concerned that they might be susceptible to connections from malicious cyber actors.”
In the warning, Wisconsin said that Minnesota had reported that hackers managed to drop system pressures, which in “several incidents triggered alarms and prompted a response from law enforcement.”
In an email, the spokesperson for Minnesota’s information technology agency disputed Wisconsin’s characterizations of the attack and its observed impacts.
“Minnesota has not reported that threat actors lowered pressure across multiple water systems or that pressure changes prompted a law enforcement response,” said the spokesperson, Emily Zimmer.
The agencies said the hackers remotely accessed internet-facing devices, changed IP addresses and passwords, and caused utilities to lose monitoring and control capabilities.

The federal advisory calls on system operators to remove programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, from direct internet exposure by putting them behind secure gateways and firewalls; use strong passwords; and limit communications between authorized control system devices through access control lists.

“Attribution requires careful analysis of technical evidence alongside broader national and international threat intelligence, and our federal partners are best positioned to lead that work,” Zimmer, the spokesperson for Minnesota’s information technology agency, said.

The breach in Minnesota happened just days after U.S. officials publicly warned that Iran-backed hackers were targeting the nation’s critical infrastructure amid the escalating military conflict between Washington and Tehran.

In a public advisory July 22, CISA, as well as the FBI and other federal agencies, urged companies to boost their defenses, saying Tehran-linked hackers were trying to breach online automated devices used to manage infrastructure systems.
U.S. intelligence agencies have also cautioned that Iran is increasingly able and willing to carry out aggressive cyber operations and that it tried to target water systems in 2023.

Bryson Bort, the founder of the cybersecurity company Scythe and an expert in industrial control system security, said the FBI’s disclosures this week underscore the need for more public awareness of the risks posed by infrastructure breaches.
“We need to be prepared,” Bort said. “Attacks like this illustrate that there are folks who mean the U.S. harm today.”

title: At least 86 dead after migrants rush into Spanish territory from Morocco
summary: Spain was scrambling Friday to contain a sudden border crisis after tens of thousands of people rushed into its North African territory, with dozens killed and political shock waves spreading across Europe.
story: Spain was scrambling Friday to contain a sudden border crisis after tens of thousands of people rushed into its North African territory, with dozens killed and political shock waves spreading across Europe.

The dramatic events were “a violation of Spain’s territorial sovereignty,” Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on a hurried visit to Ceuta, a tiny Mediterranean city at the tip of Africa that shares a border with Morocco.

Authorities in Ceuta told Sky News on Saturday that 86 people have died following the incident. The Spanish Interior Ministry earlier told NBC News that some 50,000 people had entered Ceuta on Thursday from Morocco, more than half of the city’s usual population.
Around half of that number had returned Friday, the Interior Ministry said.

title: Iran vows to ‘punish the aggressor today’ after U.S. unleashes ‘heavy wave’ of strikes
summary: The conflict appeared to draw in new countries, as Egypt confirmed that a drone hit two natural gas vessels at one of its ports.
story: Iran vowed to “punish” the United States on Thursday after the American military said it had completed a “heavy wave of strikes” overnight, the latest retaliation for an attack by Tehran on U.S. forces in the Middle East.
The renewed fighting shattered a brief period of calm that had seen the two sides engage with a push to revive diplomatic efforts and stave off dramatic new escalation.

But President Donald Trump said the U.S. would hit Iran hard after its attack on an American base in Jordan. And the powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) signaled the flare-up would not end there, warning early Thursday that “the aggressor will be punished today” following the U.S. strikes.
Jordan said it intercepted a new barrage from Iran, while Kuwait said an Iranian strike hit a building belonging to a Chinese company, killing one worker.
There were also signs that the war was again expanding and drawing in new countries, raising the stakes for the region and the global economy.
After Saudi Arabia joined the U.S. in striking Iran-backed militants in Iraq, Egypt confirmed Thursday that a drone ignited fires on two natural gas vessels at the Mediterranean port of Damietta.

Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman met with Trump and Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday to relay a message from Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that the kingdom is not looking to escalate the war with Iran, according to a source familiar with the matter.
The separate meetings came within 24 hours of the joint U.S. and Saudi strikes against Iran-backed militants in Iraq, according to a White House official.
The discussions were first reported by Axios.

In his meetings, the defense minister conveyed that the Iranian militias had crossed a line and Saudi Arabia will not tolerate anyone attacking their civilian infrastructure or energy facilities, the source said. He also emphasized that the strikes were to demonstrate Saudi Arabia’s capacity to defend itself when needed and not an indication of support for escalation.
The Saudis believe that any escalation would involve unknown risks and likely prolong the war, which is not the path they desire for the region, the source said.

It was not immediately clear who was behind the drone strikes — on a U.S.-owned floating storage facility and a Greek-owned tanker — in Egypt but an attack there by Iran would mark a significant new expansion of the conflict to a key U.S. ally and mediator. It would also highlight the broader risk to the world’s energy supplies from the difficulty in resolving the conflict.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Thursday that Egypt is an “important friend” in a post on X.

“Egypt is an important friend and partner in the region, and its security is of utmost importance to us,” he wrote. “We must all be vigilant against Israeli plots and false-flag operations designed to undermine regional peace.”
Asked if Iran was responsible for the Egypt attack during an Oval Office event Wednesday, Trump said that he had been briefed on the incident and that “it’s a little more of the same.”
“It’s going to be straightening out,” he added, without expanding on what exactly he meant. “In the meantime, we’re going to be hitting them very hard because it’s our turn to hit them.”
Trump also vowed Wednesday to “beat the f---ing s--- out of” Iran after its Tuesday attack on American forces, according to Fox News, which cited a phone call with the president.

title: U.S. strikes Iran after Trump reportedly issues menacing new threat
summary: The fighting shattered a brief period of calm after weeks of escalation between the U.S. and Iran over the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
story: The U.S. military attacked Iran on Wednesday after President Donald Trump vowed to “beat the f---ing s--- out of” the country, according to Fox News, following new attacks on American forces in the Middle East.
“They’re going to get a beating,” Trump said, according to Fox’s chief foreign correspondent, Trey Yingst.
U.S. Central Command said a “heavy wave of strikes” had been completed at 10 p.m. ET, two hours after they began.
The strikes on dozens of targets “aimed to further diminish threats posed by Iran and its proxies to American forces, commercial shipping, and neighboring Gulf countries,” the command said on X.
The comments followed what the U.S. described as a “surprise attack,” which prompted Saudi Arabia and the U.S. to retaliate against a Tehran-backed militia in Iraq.

Iran had suspended its attacks amid a renewed push to reach a deal with the U.S., but it warned this week that it would not allow Washington to dictate the “timing of war and peace” and maintained that the Strait of Hormuz was “closed.”
The sudden return of hostilities shattered the relative calm that had descended on Iran for several days after the U.S. paused daily strikes on the Islamic Republic to make room for peace talks.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it launched strikes on a U.S. air base and military central command center in Jordan, state-run Nour News agency reported early Wednesday local time. Its navy also struck three oil tankers that it said were “in violation” of its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, according to the state-run news agency IRNA.

U.S. Central Command, or CENTCOM, said on X that it had thwarted an “attempted surprise attack” on forces based in the Middle East around 5:45 p.m. Tuesday. All Iranian missiles were intercepted, it said, but troops remained “vigilant and at a high state of readiness.”

Just hours later, CENTCOM said it had launched “precision strikes” in Iraq alongside the Saudi armed forces against “Iran-aligned terrorists” that it said the IRGC had directed to attack U.S. forces and Saudi energy infrastructure.

title: K-pop group BTS won’t submit its music for Grammy Awards
summary: “I hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language,” the group said in a statement.
story: K-pop sensation BTS said Wednesday that it will not submit its music for consideration at the 2027 Grammy Awards, citing concerns over category divisions.
The seven members — RM, Jimin, V, Suga, Jungkook, Jin and j-Hope — uploaded the same statement to their individual Instagram accounts.
“We have decided not to enter the Grammys this year,” a translation of the message read. “I hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language.”

The hugely popular group from South Korea was widely expected to be nominated for some of the Recording Academy’s top accolades at the 69th Grammy Awards — including album of the year. The boyband’s most recent album, “Arirang,” has been one of the bestselling records of the year.
The album’s lead single, “Swim,” was a Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 hit in the United States.

Under the new categorizations, “Swim” might have been excluded from competing for best Asian pop music performance, one of the five new categories the Recording Academy announced last month. The new award categories were sold as an effort to boost inclusivity.

While a lot of BTS’ songs are in Korean, the lead track is mostly sung in English. A rulebook for the Grammy Awards specifies that the recordings for the new award “must feature meaningful use of one or more Asian languages.”
“An Asian language should play a significant role within the song in bilingual or multilingual structures such that the recording is identifiable with that language,” the rulebook reads.
Grammys CEO Harvey Mason Jr. said in a statement Wednesday that he was saddened by the group’s decision “but as a music creator, I understand and respect their decision.”
He said the Asian Pop category was created to celebrate “the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia.”
“More categories mean more artists’ work is recognized. It’s never to divide, but to expand who is recognized by our 15,000 Grammy voters,” Mason said.
He noted that submitting music in a specific genre category doesn’t exclude artists from also submitting and being considered  general categories, such as Song of the Year.
Mason said the Grammys will “continue to listen to the global music community and work to honor and celebrate all the artists whose music moves the world.”

BTS, which formed in 2013 and has been compared to The Beatles, has previously performed at the Grammys and was the first K-pop act to receive a Grammy nomination. It has earned five nominations but so far hasn’t won.

BTS stands for the Korean phrase “Bangtan Sonyeondan,” which translates to “Bulletproof Boy Scouts.” The band has a huge global following and recently performed in the United States during the World Cup final’s halftime show.
On Wednesday, the group thanked its fans for their support.
“Thank you to Army and everyone who is always with us,” the band said.

title: At least 13 killed in Japan earthquake as rescuers search for survivors in a ‘race against time’
summary: Multiple people were missing a day after a magnitude-7.1 quake struck Kumamoto prefecture, partially collapsing buildings.
story: At least 13 people have been killed in southwestern Japan after a magnitude-7.1 earthquake, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Wednesday, as rescuers searched for people trapped in collapsed buildings, including a shopping mall.

“Even now, there are people waiting to be rescued, and this is a race against time. We will marshal all available resources on the ground to save and rescue as many people as possible,” Takaichi told reporters in Tokyo.

The quake struck Tuesday afternoon in Kumamoto prefecture on Japan’s southern main island of Kyushu at a relatively shallow depth of 6 miles, prompting tsunami warnings and evacuation from coastal areas. The epicenter was about 12 miles south of the city of Kumamoto, which has a population of about 700,000.

While the tsunami warning was lifted shortly after, the quake caused extensive damage throughout the prefecture, including to historic buildings such as Kumamoto Castle, a popular tourist site that is still under repair from another deadly quake in the same area in 2016.
It also ruptured roads and left thousands of homes without power, with officials warning residents to beware of heatstroke as temperatures reach well into the 90s.

title: Major earthquake rocks southern Japan, injuring dozens
summary: The earthquake, which had an epicenter in the southwest part of the country, was measured at magnitude 6.8 and a depth of 10 kilometers, or just over 6 miles.
story: A 6.8-magnitude earthquake rocked southern Japan on Tuesday, forcing hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate and prompting the collapse of several buildings, including a shopping mall.
Japanese officials instructed roughly 300,000 people in the country’s southern Kumamoto prefecture to seek shelter at evacuation centers.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Wednesday morning local time that 13 people have been found dead and many other people were injured or still missing as rescue work continued overnight.

The Japan Meteorological Agency said the earthquake, with a preliminary magnitude of 7.1 and depth of just over 6 miles, was at the highest end of the seismic intensity scale. The U.S. Geological Survey later revised its measurement to magnitude 6.8. Its epicenter was about 12 miles south of Kumamoto, central Kyushu island’s largest city, with a population of around 700,000, according to officials.

The Japanese Cabinet Office’s disaster management division said the earthquake struck around 4:27 p.m. local time (3:27 a.m. ET), with a tsunami advisory issued for the Ariake and Yatsushiro seas minutes later. The warning was later lifted, state broadcaster NHK reported.

An unknown number of people were trapped in a shopping mall, according to fire officials, who said an explosion had been heard on the building’s second floor. Twenty to 30 mall employees were unaccounted for, NHK reported.

Commercial broadcaster TBS quoted local police as saying “quite a few” people are believed to have been killed after the explosion. A second broadcaster, Fuji TV, said that multiple deaths had been confirmed at the mall.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
State broadcaster NHK carried footage of almost a dozen fire trucks in the facility’s parking lot. Images also showed the mall’s collapsed ceilings and facade and a debris-littered road.
Several other buildings were also damaged, video from the region showed. At least 12 houses collapsed, and at least 50 people were injured.

Aerial footage from NHK showed that a chimney at a Nippon Paper Industries plant in Yatsushiro, a city in the Kumamoto prefecture, had partially collapsed. Local police said that several people who work at the plant are unaccounted for.
“We are gathering information on whether there are any casualties, but we are concerned because we cannot reach them,” a spokesperson for the plant told NHK.

A verified video from the city showed that a rupture on the Kyushu Expressway had trapped vehicles. NHK showed aerial images of an elevated stretch of the highway where two sections had become misaligned.
Train services around the Kyushu island were suspended, rail operator JR Kyushu said.
Takaichi said in a statement that 300 service members were being dispatched to the disaster zone.

“The government will spare no effort in emergency disaster response measures, with the highest priority placed on saving lives and rescue operations led by local police and fire departments,” her office said in a statement.
“Strong tremors, earthquakes of similar intensity may continue to occur over approximately the next week,” the statement added.

title: Search for North Carolina woman Liz Waddell is still a missing person case, Grenada police say
summary: Grenadian police said their nearly week-old search for a missing North Carolina woman is still active, with hopes of finding the swimmer alive.
story: Grenadian police said Tuesday that their nearly week-old search for a missing North Carolina woman is still active, with hopes of finding the swimmer alive.
Elizabeth “Liz” Waddell, a 44-year-old Cary resident, was last seen going out for a swim at Grand Anse Beach on Wednesday, the Royal Grenada Police Force said.

“At this time, the matter continues, continues to be treated as a missing person investigation,” acting Commissioner of Police Randy Connaught told reporters Tuesday. “I repeat, at this time, the matter continues to be treated as a missing person.”
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
Surveillance cameras captured Waddell walking on a jetty near the water at 11:36 a.m. the morning she went missing, Connaught said.
She went into the water at 11:51 a.m. and more footage captured her swimming under the jetty at 12:04 p.m., the police official said.
Witnesses have told investigators they later saw Waddell in the open water, police said.
Waddell’s traveling partner was captured on surveillance cameras on the beach at 12:46 p.m. and she reported the swimmer missing to police at 5:50 p.m., Connaught added.
“There is nothing questionable about her account of the investigations and we continue to receive cooperation from her,”  Connaught said of the traveling companion.
Even though Waddell hasn’t been seen in nearly six days, police said they still seek to rescue her.
“It is our hope that Elizabeth will be found and found alive and well,” Connaught said. “The Royal Grenada Police Force remains equally hopeful that she will be safe and that she is safe.”
Local police had been appealing to fishermen, boat operators and residents along the southern coastline to keep their eyes peeled for medium-build woman with short blond hair.
Waddell and her friend first arrived in Grenada, the island nation in the eastern Caribbean Sea that’s about 100 miles north of Venezuela, on July 11.
The missing woman’s husband has since come to the island to help in the search effort, officials said.

“Any bit of information will do at this time, and we do hope that we can locate Elizabeth very soon,” Connaught said. “Again, we empathize with the family, relatives and friends, and we are hopeful that Elizabeth will be found alive. Thank you.”

title: Oil prices slide as U.S. and Iran pause strikes to give ‘space’ for diplomacy
summary: The two sides halted fire over the weekend, following 13 nights of attacks that threatened new pain for the global economy.
story: Oil prices tumbled Monday as the United States and Iran paused their escalating strikes to make “space” for diplomacy.
The two sides halted fire over the weekend, following 13 consecutive nights of attacks that shattered their deal to end the war and threatened new pain for the global economy.
International oil benchmark Brent closed down by 8.7%, at $88.36 per barrel, while U.S. crude fell by 7.5% to $82.61 per barrel.
The moves were a sharp and rapid reversal from last week, when prices gained more than 9% and Brent rose as high as $102. Last week was oil’s third straight week of gains.

Prices fell to nearly their lowest levels of the day after President Donald Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that the U.S. was talking with Iran “right now.” He added that he was not in a rush to make a deal and had “plenty of time” for talks.

Stocks broadly rallied earlier in the day, but those gains faded as the day progressed. By late afternoon trading, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq were flat. The Dow still had a slight gain of about 200 points.
U.S. Treasury yields, which steer consumer borrowing rates, declined only slightly and were still near the highest level since early 2025.

The renewed optimism follows mounting fears of a return to all-out war across the Middle East, as the battle for control of the crucial Strait of Hormuz expanded to the Red Sea, another key waterway for global trade.
Iran has launched several drones at ships in the strait in the past several days, according to a U.S. official, who noted that the U.S. military shot down the drones and no ships were impacted.
Iranian-backed militias also continue to target U.S. interests, U.S. forces and partners in Iraq, the official said. The U.S. has also been defending against those attacks.
Trump said Thursday that he was considering a “massive attack” to try to break Iran’s grip on the strait, but since then the U.S. and Iran have refrained from attacks for three days.
The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday that the decision to halt strikes came in response to ongoing talks between the two sides.

“What the president is doing right now, as we’ve seen all along, is giving some talks some space,” he said, adding that talks were “ongoing” but that there was “internal fighting” on the Iranian side.
Waltz dismissed reporting that U.S. weapons stockpiles are depleted.
Still, Tehran offered limited hope for any ramped-up peace efforts.

“Mediators may convey messages from the American side to us concerning regional developments, but at the present time we have no negotiations with the American side,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday at a news conference.
He said Tehran would “never allow America to determine the timing of war and peace” and would “continue to defend ourselves for as long as our interests and considerations require.”
Baghaei maintained that the Strait of Hormuz was “closed.”

Oil prices had soared above $100 per barrel last week for the first time in two months as the conflict spiraled, with Hormuz effectively blocked and new disruption from attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in the Red Sea.
Shipping traffic through Hormuz was limited over the weekend, with more activity visible through the Bab el Mandeb choke point.

Along the Strait of Hormuz, just 29 verified transits were recorded from Friday to Sunday, according to an NBC News analysis of MarineTraffic data. Activity fell from 12 crossings Friday to six Saturday, before increasing to 11 Sunday.
Traffic along Bab el Mandeb remained higher, with 100 verified crossings over the same period. Daily activity was broadly stable, with 35 crossings Friday, 31 Saturday and 34 Sunday.
Prior to the war, some 20% of the world’s oil had passed through the Strait of Hormuz, with its repeated closure sending energy prices soaring and global markets tumbling throughout the conflict.
“The market seems to be forever seeking good news from an arena that really is not providing any,” PVM analyst John Evans said.

“A stay of military strikes might seem an improvement, but it does not come with any guarantees that oil will soon flow from the area. ... Prices will only continue lower if high prices once again dent demand, not questionable mini-ceasefires,” Evans said.

On Monday, the semiofficial Iranian Tasnim news agency reported that six vessels had attempted to pass through Hormuz “by switching off their navigation and position systems.” It said one of them “suffered an incident” while the others were returned to the Persian Gulf “under Iran’s decisive management.”

Jordan, a key U.S. ally, said it downed two drones early Monday, though it was not clear who launched them. Saudi Arabia said it intercepted and destroyed drones fired by Iran-backed militants in Iraq.
Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu made his way to Washington on Monday, with plans to discuss Iran in a meeting with Trump set for Tuesday.
“Our objective is to safeguard our security while also expanding the circle of peace around us,” Netanyahu said in comments prior to his departure.

He also noted that he was traveling to the U.S. to pay his final respects at the funeral of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., whom Netanyahu described as “one of the greatest friends Israel has ever had.”
Beyond the Middle East, attacks between Russia and Ukraine have also increasingly focused on shipping, adding another complication for markets.

The Iranian Foreign Ministry accused Ukraine over the weekend of attacking an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea, saying one sailor was killed and another injured. The ministry summoned Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires in Tehran in protest.
